nameStory: The "tick-trefoil" name comes from this plant's notorious hitchhiking seeds that stick to clothing and fur just like ticks do! The "stiff" part refers to its upright, rigid stems that don't bend easily in the wind. Like other trefoils, it has three-part leaves that reminded early botanists of clover.
description: Stiff tick-trefoil is an upright wildflower in the legume family, standing 1-3 feet tall with sturdy, unbending stems. It produces small pink to purple pea-like flowers in summer, followed by flat, segmented seed pods that break apart into sticky pieces. The three-part leaves and upright growth habit make it look like a taller, stiffer version of clover. As a legume, it helps enrich the soil by fixing nitrogen through its root bacteria.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems are notably rigid and upright, feeling stiff and woody when you gently bend them - they resist bending much more than other tick-trefoils

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-leaflet leaves (like clover) with oval leaflets that feel smooth and somewhat thick, arranged alternately up the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-shaped flowers about 1/4 inch long, clustered in narrow spikes at the stem tips during summer

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, jointed seed pods that break into triangular segments covered in tiny hooked hairs that grab onto clothing and feel scratchy to the touch

habitat: Stiff tick-trefoil grows in dry, open areas like prairies, old fields, and woodland edges with sandy or well-drained soils. In New England, look for it in sunny spots with poor to average soil where other plants might struggle. It's quite rare in our region, preferring the warmer climates further south.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the three-part leaves unfurl from the base, looking like tiny clover plants at first.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from July through August, with the characteristic pink pea-flowers clustered at stem tips.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and begin breaking apart into their sticky segments that cling to anything passing by. Leaves may turn yellowish.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems remain standing and stiff, often still holding some persistent seed pod fragments.

funFact: The sticky seed segments are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired the invention of Velcro - a Swiss engineer got the idea after pulling countless burrs like these off his dog's fur!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tick-trefoils, but the notably stiff, rigid stems set it apart - other species have more flexible, bendable stems. Remember: "stiff name, stiff stems!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "stiff tick-trefoil," this plant is actually quite rare in New England with only one documented observation, making it more of a southern species that just barely reaches our region. Don't expect to find it on every nature walk!
compareHints: Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily. It's also typically shorter and more compact than the tall tick-trefoils, with a stiffer overall appearance even when not in bloom.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
